messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: inits for test models?
parts:
I'm going through the remaining BUGS models to see if we can get them all running in Stan.

vol2/schools converges to the right answer quickly with init=0, but takes 500 or so iterations to converge with random inits (they ran BUGS with 10K iterations for this example). It's also not the fastest model.

The initializations provided with JAGS are only partial, which we don't have working yet for Stan. Can we set the test to zero init, or should I hand code an init file?

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] inits for test models?
parts:
I'd prefer to avoid inits of 0.000. If you think our default inits tend to create problems, we could switch to uniform(-.5,.5) or something like that?
I hope that our new multi-stage adaptation will solve this problem, in any case.
A

P.S. If we're ever recoding a Bugs model and it runs slow and there are any easy fixes (e.g., the Matt trick), we should just put the fix in. We might as well make Stan look as fast as possible.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] inits for test models?
parts:
On June 15, 2013 09:05:24 PM EDT, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> I'd prefer to avoid inits of 0.000. If you think our default inits
> tend to create problems, we could switch to uniform(-.5,.5) or
> something like that?

We could. Right now, Michael's working on the new commands,
so that'd be the natural place to put it. Marcus has also
requested more control over inits in the past.

In the past, you (Andrew) said to just use the BUGS inits.
In many cases, these are themselves 0.

What I'd like to have eventually is user-specified inits
with a degree of randomization around them.

> I hope that our new multi-stage adaptation will solve this problem,
> in any case.
That'd be nice. :-)

> P.S. If we're ever recoding a Bugs model and it runs slow and there
> are any easy fixes (e.g., the Matt trick), we should just put the fix
> in. We might as well make Stan look as fast as possible.

Anything we do with these globally is a pain because there
are dozens and dozens of them.

It's also not clear the "Matt trick" is always a win. So
it's going to take some work to find the optimal way to fit
these models in Stan. That all seems a bit unfair for comparison
unless we do the same for BUGS/JAGS implementations.

We had decided a meeting or two ago that we'd try to build

both a direct translation and a more idiomatic Stan version.
That would allow both the direct comparison, whatever that means, and also
a comparison with a more optimized Stan implementations.

Right now, the models are all over the place in terms of
how much vectorization and other efficiency coding.
If we try to conform to the plan of a baseline and a fast
version, it's going to be a lot of work, because there are
dozens and dozens of models, none of which have very extensive
doc either on the Stan or BUGS side.

Right now, I'm just trying to get them all working and
getting the same answers.

We wanted to compare to JAGS. To do that with our diffuse
inits, we'd need to take those diffuse inits, constrain them,
then feed them into JAGS. Right now, most of the BUGS models
get hard-coded inits. In my experience, many models won't
fit in either Stan or BUGS without reasonable inits.

We also haven't decided what to do about their priors.
The BUGS examples are full of really fat priors, like normal(0,1000)

for parameters with values in single digits.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] inits for test models?
parts:
On Jun 15, 2013, at 9:15 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:


In the past, you (Andrew) said to just use the BUGS inits.
In many cases, these are themselves 0.

I'm happy to use the Bugs inits when doing head-to-head comparisons, but (a) you said that in some models they don't fully specify the inits, and (b) I don't want 0.000 as a general option; it just seems to me that this could cause trouble.

What I'd like to have eventually is user-specified inits
with a degree of randomization around them.
Yes, I agree that users should be able to specify inits.  But we do need defaults.

P.S.  If we're ever recoding a Bugs model and it runs slow and there
are any easy fixes (e.g., the Matt trick), we should just put the fix
in.  We might as well make Stan look as fast as possible.

Anything we do with these globally is a pain because there
are dozens and dozens of them.

I'm not saying we should do these globally.  All I'm saying is, if we have a _particular_ model that is running relatively slowly in Stan, _and_ we happen to see an _easy_ way to make it faster, we can just do it.

It's also not clear the "Matt trick" is always a win.  So
it's going to take some work to find the optimal way to fit
these models in Stan.
I'm not talking about optimal, I'm just saying that we should feel free to spiff up slow models if that's easy to do.

That all seems a bit unfair for comparison
unless we do the same for BUGS/JAGS implementations.
I disagree.  We're already playing on Bugs's turf/

Right now, the models are all over the place in terms of
how much vectorization and other efficiency coding.
If we try to conform to the plan of a baseline and a fast
version, it's going to be a lot of work, because there are
dozens and dozens of models, none of which have very extensive
doc either on the Stan or BUGS side.
I am not saying we should optimize all the models; I'm just saying that, when we're doing the implementations, we can feel free to make them faster if it's not too difficult.

Right now, I'm just trying to get them all working and
getting the same answers.

I agree, that's the #1 issue.  Then when we have the scatterplot showing the speed comparisons, if there are any dots on the plot that make Stan look bad, I think it would be ok to take a quick look and see if some vectorization or reparameterization will make it go faster.

We wanted to compare to JAGS.  To do that with our diffuse
inits, we'd need to take those diffuse inits, constrain them,
then feed them into JAGS.  Right now, most of the BUGS models
get hard-coded inits.  In my experience, many models won't
fit in either Stan or BUGS without reasonable inits.
In that case we can use the Jags inits.  And when Jags doesn't fully specify inits, we will have to specify them.

We also haven't decided what to do about their priors.
The BUGS examples are full of really fat priors, like normal(0,1000)

for parameters with values in single digits.
We should probably stick with those for our models too, no?

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] inits for test models?
parts:
On Sunday, June 16, 2013 3:38:06 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
Changing the command to init=a to do random inits between -a and a would be extremely easy.

I agree and suggested that we do that a while ago, which is probably fine for model testing. But speaking more generally about initial values, it would be good to have an option to draw a uniform on the support of parameter and transform it to unbounded, but that only works well when the support is bounded on both sides. The best would be to support an init block in the .stan file where users could draw from their priors or specify some subset of the initial values nonrandomly, and convert that to unbounded.

Ben

parts:
We've already discussed that any model that has finite mass at a boundary would not be appropriate for HMC, the easiest way of thinking about it being that after we transform variables such model would have finite mass at +/- infinity, which we certainly can't handle on a computer. So trying to sample randomly between bounds is a bad idea -- we want to sample uniformly from the typical set, not the entire support.

It looks like -2, 2 is indeed too big for the uninitialized BUGS models, so smaller is probably better. We can always try small values, [-1, 1] or [-1/2, 1/2], see how the ensemble of models performs.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] inits for test models?
parts:
On Sunday, June 16, 2013 6:49:34 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
We've already discussed that any model that has finite mass at a boundary would not be appropriate for HMC, the easiest way of thinking about it being that after we transform variables such model would have finite mass at +/- infinity, which we certainly can't handle on a computer.
I agree with that, but that seems like problem that is broader than just choosing starting values.
So trying to sample randomly between bounds is a bad idea -- we want to sample uniformly from the typical set, not the entire support.

You could draw uniformally on half the width of the support if you like that better, but the best thing would be to make it easy for the user to specify (some subset of) initial values, possibly random draws from the prior, in an init block of the .stan file.

It looks like -2, 2 is indeed too big for the uninitialized BUGS models, so smaller is probably better.  We can always try small values, [-1, 1] or [-1/2, 1/2], see how the ensemble of models performs.

Uniform on (-a,a) with a chosen by the user is better than hard-coding a = 2, but there are so many different transformations that it is hard to set a width on the unbounded scale and have that be good for each bounded parameter. But it would be a step in the right direction. Right now, we have too many situations where we have to start with init=0 just to avoid the initial (-2,2) behavior that ruins the convergence.

Ben
